title: Roman Stoicism: Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius
subtitle: A millionaire, a former slave and an emperor discover the same freedom
objectives: By the end you will be able to describe the lives and main works of Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius
Explain the dichotomy of control and how it applies Stoic theory from Day 25 to everyday life
Describe Stoic spiritual exercises such as premeditatio malorum, the evening review and the view from above
Assess the charge of hypocrisy against Seneca and the charge of political passivity against Stoicism
Explain how Stoicism influenced cognitive behavioral therapy and where the modern comparison breaks down
hook:
Imagine three people. One is among the richest men in the Roman Empire, a playwright and the chief adviser to the emperor Nero. One was born into slavery in a remote province, walks with a limp and owns almost nothing. One is the emperor himself, the most powerful man in the known world, writing private notes to himself in a tent on the cold Danube frontier during a long war.

They could hardly be more different. Yet all three were Stoics, and all three asked the same question: in a world where fortune can take everything, from your wealth to your freedom to your life, what remains truly yours? Yesterday you met the theory: virtue is the only good, everything else is indifferent, and passions are mistaken judgments. Today you will see how Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius turned that theory into a daily practice, one that still sells millions of books and that helped inspire one of the most widely used forms of psychotherapy in the world.

sections.heading: From Athens to Rome
sections.body:
Stoicism reached Rome in the second century BCE. You will meet one of the key moments on Day 27: in 155 BCE, Athens sent three philosophers as ambassadors to Rome, including the Stoic Diogenes of Babylon. Later Stoics such as Panaetius (c. 185–109 BCE) and Posidonius softened some of the school's harder doctrines and made it attractive to Roman aristocrats. Panaetius, for example, focused less on the perfect sage and more on the person making progress, and wrote about the different roles each of us plays in life.

The Romans were practical people, and Roman Stoicism became, above all, a philosophy of practice. The great Roman Stoics were less interested in logic and physics than Chrysippus had been, though they never abandoned them. They wanted to know how to face exile, illness, grief, anger and death. The texts that survive from this period, unlike the lost works of the early Stoa, are the reason most people today know Stoicism at all.

One more figure deserves mention: **Musonius Rufus** (c. 30–100 CE), a Roman Stoic teacher exiled more than once by emperors. His lectures, preserved by a student, include striking arguments that women should study philosophy because they have the same reason and the same capacity for virtue as men, and that daughters should receive the same education as sons. Musonius' most famous student was a young slave named Epictetus.

sections.heading: Seneca: The Philosopher at Court
sections.body:
**Lucius Annaeus Seneca** (c. 4 BCE–65 CE) was born in Corduba, in Roman Spain, to a wealthy family. He became a celebrated orator and writer in Rome, survived a death sentence under the emperor Caligula (according to one ancient report, because Caligula was told he would soon die of illness anyway), and was exiled to Corsica by the emperor Claudius in 41 CE. Recalled in 49 CE, he became tutor to the young Nero and, when Nero became emperor in 54 CE, one of his chief advisers.

For several years Seneca and the guard commander Burrus helped steer the empire. But Nero grew increasingly violent; he had his own mother murdered in 59 CE, and Seneca was implicated at least in the aftermath. Seneca withdrew from court around 62 CE. In 65 CE, accused of involvement in a conspiracy against Nero, he was ordered to kill himself. The historian Tacitus describes his death, in which he consoled his weeping friends and reminded them of the philosophy they had studied.

Seneca wrote essays such as *On Anger*, *On the Shortness of Life* and *On Tranquillity of Mind*, as well as tragedies, but his masterpiece is the *Letters to Lucilius*, 124 letters on how to live, written in his last years. They are warm, witty and personal. He writes about crowds, travel, friendship, old age and fear, and he freely quotes Epicurus when he finds him wise, saying that he likes to cross into the enemy's camp, not as a deserter but as a scout.

In one letter he observes that we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. His remedy, built on the early Stoic view that passions are judgments, was to examine those judgments calmly and in advance.

Seneca has long faced the **charge of hypocrisy**. He praised poverty while owning a vast fortune, gained partly through lending at interest; he preached virtue while serving Nero. His critics, ancient and modern, have not let him forget it. Seneca's own answer, in *On the Happy Life*, was that he was not a sage but a man trying to improve, and that wealth is a preferred indifferent the wise may hold, provided they could lose it without distress. Whether you accept that defence is one of the questions of this lesson.

sections.heading: Epictetus: Freedom in Chains
sections.body:
**Epictetus** (c. 50–c. 135 CE) was born a slave in Hierapolis, in Phrygia (in modern Turkey). His name simply means 'acquired'. He was owned by Epaphroditus, a freedman who served Nero, and was allowed to study with Musonius Rufus. He was lame; one later story says his master twisted his leg until it broke while Epictetus calmly warned that it would break, but other ancient sources say the lameness came from illness, so treat the story as legend.

At some point he was freed and began teaching philosophy in Rome. Around 93 CE, the emperor Domitian expelled philosophers from the city, and Epictetus moved to Nicopolis, in north-western Greece, where he ran a school until his death. Like Socrates, he wrote nothing. His student Arrian, later a distinguished historian, recorded his lectures in the *Discourses*, four books of which survive, and condensed the core teaching into a short *Handbook*, the *Enchiridion*.

The *Handbook* opens with the idea that defines Epictetus' Stoicism, the **dichotomy of control**. Some things are up to us, and some are not. Up to us are our judgments, our impulses, our desires and aversions: in a word, our own actions of mind. Not up to us are our body, our property, our reputation, our position: in a word, everything that is not our own doing. The things up to us are by nature free; the things not up to us are weak, slavish and belong to others.

This is early Stoicism (Day 25) made practical. The faculty of choice, which Epictetus called **prohairesis**, is the one thing that is truly yours. A tyrant can chain your leg, Epictetus says, but not even Zeus can overpower your choice. A former slave was uniquely placed to say this. He knew from experience that legal freedom and inner freedom are different, and that a powerful man can be a slave to his fears and desires.

The fifth section of the *Handbook* contains Epictetus' most famous line, the one that would inspire modern psychotherapy, quoted below. His example is death. Death is not terrible; otherwise it would have seemed terrible to Socrates (Day 10). What is terrible is our judgment that death is terrible.

Epictetus was also a fierce teacher. He mocked students who wanted to be admired for knowing Chrysippus while still panicking over small losses. Philosophy, he insisted, is shown in how you handle a broken cup, an insult or a storm at sea, not in how many books you can quote.

sections.heading: Marcus Aurelius: Notes to Himself
sections.body:
**Marcus Aurelius** (121–180 CE) was emperor of Rome from 161 CE until his death. He had studied philosophy since youth and was deeply influenced by the *Discourses* of Epictetus, which a teacher had lent him. His reign was hard: a devastating epidemic known as the Antonine Plague spread across the empire, and he spent many years fighting Germanic peoples along the Danube.

During those campaigns he wrote, in Greek, a private notebook. Its original title, if it had one, may have been something like *To Himself*. We call it the ***Meditations***. It was never meant for publication. It is a set of reminders, repeated again and again, of the Stoic principles he was trying to live by. That is what makes it so moving: we are reading a powerful man's struggle to be good.

Book 1 is a list of gratitude, thanking the people from whom he learned something: his grandfather for good character, his mother for simplicity, his teachers for lessons in patience and frankness. Book 2 opens with a famous morning exercise. Tell yourself at the start of the day, he writes, that you will meet people who are meddling, ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious and unsociable. They are like this because they do not know good from evil. But they are your kin, sharing the same reason, and you cannot be harmed by them or be angry with them, because we are made to work together, like feet, hands or eyelids.

Recurring themes include the brevity of life, the constant change of all things (he often echoes Heraclitus, Day 4), the duty to serve the common good, and acceptance of whatever the whole of nature brings. In one passage often quoted today, he observes that the obstacle to action can advance action, and that what stands in the way can become the way. That is a modern paraphrase of Book 5, section 20, but it captures his point: a difficulty is material for virtue.

Marcus is not beyond criticism. He named his son Commodus as heir, and Commodus proved to be a disastrous emperor. Christians were persecuted in parts of the empire during his reign, as in the martyrdoms at Lyon in 177 CE, though historians debate his personal role. Philosophy did not make him perfect, as he himself would have been the first to admit.

sections.heading: Spiritual Exercises
sections.body:
The historian of philosophy Pierre Hadot called the Stoic practices **spiritual exercises**: techniques for transforming how you see and feel, not just what you believe. Here are four of the most important.

1. **Premeditatio malorum**, the 'premeditation of evils'. Imagine in advance the misfortunes that could happen: loss of money, illness, exile, the death of loved ones. Seneca recommended this so that nothing would take us by surprise. The point is not to wallow but to rehearse calm, to see that such events are part of nature, and to appreciate what we have while we have it. Epictetus gave a startling version: when you kiss your child, remind yourself that she is mortal.
2. **The evening review**. Seneca describes how, each night, after the lamp was put out, he examined his whole day: where had he acted badly, where well, what could he do better? He borrowed the practice from an earlier philosopher named Sextius.
3. **The view from above**. Marcus repeatedly imagines looking down on human life from a great height: armies, farms, weddings, funerals, markets, all tiny and brief against the vastness of space and time. Seen this way, our anxieties and ambitions shrink to their proper size.
4. **Voluntary discomfort**. Seneca advises setting aside a few days to live on the cheapest food and coarsest clothing, asking yourself whether this is what you feared. Here you can hear the Cynics' askesis (Day 23), tamed into a periodic exercise.

These practices answer a common objection to Stoicism: that knowing the theory is not enough. The Stoics agreed. You cannot simply decide to stop fearing death; you have to train, daily, as an athlete trains. And they answer a second objection, that Stoicism is cold, by showing what the exercises aim at. They are designed to make you more grateful, more patient with others and more able to act well under pressure.

But a fair critic presses on. Does focusing on what is 'up to us' encourage passive acceptance of injustice? Marcus never questioned slavery or empire. Defenders reply that Stoicism demands action, since justice is a virtue, and that it governs how we act, not whether we act. Many Stoics, including Seneca, Musonius and other senators who opposed tyrants, paid for their convictions with exile or death.

keyQuote.text: Men are disturbed not by things, but by the views which they take of things.

modernConnection.title: From the Handbook to the Therapist's Office
modernConnection.body:
In the 1950s, the psychologist Albert Ellis developed what became Rational Emotive Behavior Therapy, and in the 1960s the psychiatrist Aaron Beck developed cognitive therapy. Both rest on an idea Epictetus would recognise at once: our emotional suffering is shaped by our interpretations of events, and if we identify and test those interpretations, we can feel and act differently. Ellis often cited Epictetus' line about being disturbed by our views of things, and Beck and his colleagues, in their influential 1979 book *Cognitive Therapy of Depression*, traced the philosophical origins of cognitive therapy to the Stoics. Today **cognitive behavioral therapy** (CBT) is among the most studied psychological treatments for anxiety and depression.

The parallels are close. A CBT client learns to notice an 'automatic thought' (I will be fired, it will be a catastrophe), examine the evidence and replace it with a more accurate thought. That is a modern version of the Stoic practice of examining impressions before assenting. Exposure techniques echo premeditatio malorum and voluntary discomfort. And the Serenity Prayer, associated with the theologian Reinhold Niebuhr and used in Alcoholics Anonymous, asks for the serenity to accept what we cannot change and the courage to change what we can, a close cousin of the dichotomy of control.

Stoicism has also become a popular movement. Books such as Ryan Holiday's *The Obstacle Is the Way* (2014), named after the Marcus passage you read today, have sold millions of copies, and since 2012 researchers and therapists have run an annual online 'Stoic Week'. Prisoners, soldiers and athletes have adopted it; the US Navy pilot James Stockdale credited Epictetus with helping him survive more than seven years as a prisoner of war in Vietnam.

The comparison breaks down in important ways. CBT does not ask you to believe that virtue is the only good or that the universe is governed by a rational providence. It asks whether thoughts are accurate and helpful, not whether they are virtuous. And some popular 'Stoicism', especially online, reduces it to emotional toughness and productivity hacks for ambitious individuals, forgetting that the ancient Stoics saw justice and duty to all humanity as central. Marcus' morning exercise is about treating difficult people as kin, not about winning.

vocabulary.definition: Epictetus' division of all things into those that are up to us (our judgments, desires and choices) and those that are not (body, property, reputation, others' actions).
vocabulary.example: Applying the dichotomy of control, she focused on preparing well for the interview rather than worrying about the other candidates.

vocabulary.definition: Epictetus' term for the faculty of choice or moral will, the one thing that is truly our own and that no external power can compel.
vocabulary.example: Epictetus said that even Zeus could not overpower his prohairesis.

vocabulary.definition: The 'premeditation of evils': the Stoic exercise of imagining possible misfortunes in advance in order to face them calmly and appreciate the present.
vocabulary.example: Before a long trip, he practised premeditatio malorum by imagining missed flights and lost luggage, and stayed calm when it happened.

vocabulary.definition: Pierre Hadot's term for the practices ancient philosophers used to transform how they perceived and felt, such as the evening review and the view from above.
vocabulary.example: Writing in a journal each night about what you did well and badly is a modern form of an ancient spiritual exercise.

vocabulary.definition: A Stoic exercise, frequent in Marcus Aurelius, of imagining human affairs from a great height or across vast time, to put personal worries in perspective.
vocabulary.example: Looking at a photograph of Earth from space can work like the Stoic view from above.

vocabulary.definition: Marcus Aurelius' private notebook of Stoic reminders, written in Greek during his military campaigns and never intended for publication.
vocabulary.example: In the Meditations, the emperor repeatedly reminds himself to be patient with difficult people.

vocabulary.definition: The 'Handbook', a short summary of Epictetus' teaching compiled by his student Arrian, beginning with the dichotomy of control.
vocabulary.example: The Enchiridion was small enough for a soldier or a traveller to carry everywhere.

vocabulary.definition: A modern form of psychotherapy, developed from the work of Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis, that treats emotional problems by identifying and testing unhelpful thoughts and changing behaviour; its founders acknowledged a debt to the Stoics.
vocabulary.example: A CBT therapist might ask an anxious client what evidence supports the thought that one mistake will ruin her career.

thinkingExercise.title: A Stoic Day
thinkingExercise.prompt: Try three Roman Stoic exercises over the next day, and then judge whether they helped. If you prefer, do them all now in imagination.
steps: Morning (Marcus): write down two or three difficult people or situations you are likely to face today. Then write one sentence reminding yourself why the other person might act as they do, and how you want to respond.
During the day (Epictetus): when something upsets you, pause and ask whether it is up to you. Note one example of something that was not, and how you responded.

Premeditation (Seneca): choose one realistic misfortune you fear, such as losing your job, an illness or a broken phone. Imagine it happening in detail for two minutes. What would you still have? What could you still do?
Evening (Seneca): review the day. Where did you act well? Where badly? What will you do differently tomorrow?

Assess: did these exercises make you calmer, kinder, more anxious or more passive? Write a short paragraph on whether you would keep any of them, and whether the dichotomy of control ever risks making you accept something you should change.

summary: Roman Stoicism was above all practical; its surviving texts by Seneca, Epictetus and Marcus Aurelius are why most people know Stoicism today.
Seneca, Nero's wealthy adviser, wrote the Letters to Lucilius and essays on anger and the shortness of life; he faces a lasting charge of hypocrisy and was forced to die in 65 CE.
Epictetus, a former slave, taught the dichotomy of control: only our judgments, desires and choices are up to us, and people are disturbed not by things but by their views of things.
Marcus Aurelius, emperor from 161 to 180 CE, wrote the Meditations as private reminders to be patient, just and accepting of nature's order.
Stoic spiritual exercises include premeditatio malorum, the evening review, the view from above and voluntary discomfort.
Ellis and Beck acknowledged Stoicism as a philosophical root of cognitive therapy, but CBT drops Stoic claims about virtue and providence, and pop Stoicism often forgets justice.

quiz.question: According to Epictetus, which of the following is 'up to us'?
options: Our reputation
Our health
Our judgments about what happens
Whether other people treat us fairly
quiz.explanation: In the opening of the Handbook, only our judgments, impulses, desires and aversions are up to us. Body, property and reputation are not.

quiz.question: Which Roman Stoic was born a slave and later taught at Nicopolis?
options: Seneca
Marcus Aurelius
Panaetius
Epictetus
quiz.explanation: Epictetus was born a slave in Phrygia, studied with Musonius Rufus, and moved his school to Nicopolis after Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome.

quiz.question: What is premeditatio malorum?
options: Imagining possible misfortunes in advance so as to meet them calmly
Planning revenge against one's enemies
A legal procedure in Roman courts
Reviewing one's day each evening
quiz.explanation: The premeditation of evils rehearses misfortunes in imagination. The evening review is a different exercise, which Seneca also practised.

quiz.question: Why is the Meditations of Marcus Aurelius so unusual as a work of philosophy?
options: It was written in Latin verse
It was a private notebook of reminders, never intended for publication
It was dictated to a student, like the Discourses
It is a systematic treatise on Stoic logic
quiz.explanation: Marcus wrote the Meditations in Greek for himself, often during military campaigns, as a way of reminding himself of Stoic principles.

quiz.question: A client in therapy is taught to notice the thought 'If I make a mistake in this presentation, my career is over', examine the evidence, and replace it with a more realistic thought. Which Stoic idea does this most closely resemble?
options: Living according to nature by giving up possessions
The cosmic conflagration
Oikeiosis
Epictetus' claim that we are disturbed not by things but by our judgments about them
quiz.explanation: This is a standard cognitive therapy technique, and its founders explicitly traced its roots to the Stoic idea that our judgments, not events, disturb us.

quiz.question: What is the main charge often brought against Seneca?
options: Hypocrisy: he praised simplicity and virtue while amassing a vast fortune and serving Nero
Atheism: he denied the existence of the gods
Laziness: he never wrote anything
Cowardice: he fled Rome to avoid Nero
quiz.explanation: Seneca's great wealth and his service to Nero have long been held against him. He replied that he was a learner, not a sage, and that wealth is a preferred indifferent.

quiz.question: What does Marcus Aurelius' morning exercise in Book 2 of the Meditations ask him to do?
options: Rise before dawn and fast until evening
Prepare to meet difficult people, remembering that they are his kin and cannot truly harm him
Recite the laws of Rome
Imagine his own funeral in detail
quiz.explanation: He reminds himself that he will meet meddling, ungrateful and arrogant people, who act from ignorance of good and evil and who share in the same reason, so he should not be angry with them.

quiz.question: Musonius Rufus argued that women should study philosophy because they share the same reason and capacity for virtue as men.
quiz.explanation: Lectures by Musonius preserved by a student argue that women, having the same rational faculties, should study philosophy and that daughters should be educated like sons.

quiz.question: The story that Epictetus' master deliberately broke his leg is firmly established historical fact.
quiz.explanation: The story appears in a later source, while other ancient writers say his lameness came from illness. It is best treated as a legend that illustrates his calm.

quiz.question: Cognitive behavioral therapy requires patients to accept the Stoic view that virtue is the only good.
quiz.explanation: CBT borrows the Stoic insight about the role of judgments in emotion but does not require any Stoic beliefs about virtue, the indifferents or divine providence.

goDeeper.body:
Is Stoic 'acceptance' wisdom or resignation? This is the central debate about Roman Stoicism today. The dichotomy of control seems to tell us to focus on our inner life and accept the rest. Critics from Hegel (Day 59) onward have suggested that Stoicism flourishes when people feel powerless, offering inner freedom as a consolation for outer slavery. Hegel described Stoic freedom as a freedom of thought that remains abstract, withdrawing from the real world.

Defenders reply that this misreads the texts. For Epictetus, the outcome of our actions is not up to us, but the actions themselves are, and Stoic virtue includes justice and a duty to serve the common good. The philosopher William Irvine, in *A Guide to the Good Life* (2009), proposed a 'trichotomy of control': things we control completely, things we do not control at all, and things we partly control, such as winning a tennis match, where we should set internal goals like playing our best. Scholars have pointed out that Epictetus' own dichotomy already makes room for this, since our efforts are up to us.

Another debate concerns Pierre Hadot's influential reading of Marcus Aurelius in *The Inner Citadel*. Hadot argued that the *Meditations* is not a diary of a melancholy man, as earlier readers thought, but a structured set of exercises built around three Stoic disciplines he found in Epictetus: of desire, of action and of assent. Some scholars think Hadot imposed too neat a structure; others find it illuminating.

Finally, Seneca's literary achievement deserves attention. His tragedies, full of violent passion, were a major influence on Elizabethan drama, including Shakespeare's contemporaries. Why a Stoic would write plays about uncontrolled rage is itself a fascinating puzzle: perhaps as warnings, showing what happens when passion wins.

readings.title: Meditations
readings.author: Marcus Aurelius
readings.note: Gregory Hays' modern translation (Modern Library, 2002) is very readable. Start with Books 2 and 4.

readings.title: Handbook (Enchiridion) and Discourses
readings.author: Epictetus
readings.note: The Handbook takes under an hour to read. Robin Hard's Oxford World's Classics translation includes the Discourses too.

readings.title: Letters on Ethics: To Lucilius
readings.author: Seneca
readings.note: The complete letters, translated by Margaret Graver and A. A. Long (Chicago, 2015). Try Letters 7, 13, 18 and 47 (on slaves).

readings.title: The Inner Citadel: The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius
readings.author: Pierre Hadot
readings.note: For the ambitious: the classic study of Marcus' spiritual exercises and their roots in Epictetus.

questions: Can a philosopher's teaching be valuable even if their life falls short of it, as Seneca's arguably did? Does hypocrisy discredit an argument?
Does the dichotomy of control make people more effective at changing the world, or more willing to accept injustice?
Is modern 'pop Stoicism' a faithful revival or a distortion? What would Epictetus think of it?
